h1: Texas HOA Harassment by Board Member Demand Letter
metaTitle: Texas HOA Board Harassment Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a Texas HOA harassment by board member demand letter citing Property Code Chapter 209. Stop abusive conduct and protect your homeowner rights.
statuteCitation: Tex. Prop. Code Ann. §§ 209.001-209.0205 (Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act)
deadline: Owner may request a board hearing within 30 days after the enforcement notice is mailed (Tex. Prop. Code § 209.006(b)(2)(B))
penalty: Injunctive relief and damages in court; civil penalties and punitive damages are available only under specific statutes such as the Texas Fair Housing Act (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.153)
introParagraph: If you live in a Texas neighborhood governed by an HOA, you are protected by some of the strongest homeowner laws in the country. The Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act (Chapter 209 of the Property Code) sets clear rules board members must follow when communicating with, fining, or enforcing rules against owners. When a board member crosses the line into harassment—through threats, retaliatory fines, selective enforcement, surveillance, or repeated unwanted contact—Texas law gives you the right to demand it stop. A properly drafted demand letter that cites the correct Texas statutes puts the association on notice, creates a paper trail for litigation, and often resolves the issue without a lawsuit.
lawExplanation: Texas regulates HOA conduct primarily through Chapter 209 of the Texas Property Code, known as the Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act. This law applies to most single-family residential subdivisions and imposes strict procedural requirements before a board can fine, suspend privileges, foreclose, or otherwise act against an owner. Section 209.006 requires written notice by verified mail, and a reasonable period to cure a curable violation, before the association may levy a fine, suspend common-area rights, or file most suits. Section 209.007 gives owners the right to request a hearing before the board. When a board member abuses these processes—by issuing baseless violations, threatening foreclosure without basis, contacting an owner outside official channels, or retaliating for protected activity like running for the board, requesting records, or attending meetings—they may be acting outside the scope of their authority. Texas Business Organizations Code Chapter 22 governs nonprofit corporations, which includes most HOAs, and Section 22.221 requires a director to discharge the director's duties in good faith, with ordinary care, and in a manner the director reasonably believes to be in the best interest of the corporation. A board member who harasses an owner may have acted outside those standards. Additionally, Texas Penal Code § 42.07 makes it an offense to send repeated electronic communications in a manner reasonably likely to harass, annoy, alarm, abuse, torment, embarrass, or offend another, among other forms of harassment, when done with intent to harass. Owners also have rights under Section 209.005 to inspect association records and under Section 209.0051 to attend open board meetings—rights that cannot be punished. If the harassment involves discrimination based on race, religion, sex, familial status, disability, or national origin, the federal Fair Housing Act and the Texas Fair Housing Act (Chapter 301 of the Property Code) provide additional remedies, including actual and punitive damages and attorney fees in a civil action under Section 301.153.
letterStrategy: A Texas HOA harassment demand letter works because it forces the association and its insurance carrier to take the dispute seriously and document a response. The letter should identify the specific board member, describe each harassing act with dates and witnesses, and tie that conduct to violations of Chapter 209, the director's duties under Business Organizations Code Section 22.221, and the association's own governing documents. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, to both the registered agent of the HOA and the management company, and copy the full board so individual directors cannot later claim ignorance. Demand specific relief: cessation of contact outside official channels, withdrawal of any retaliatory fines or violation notices, recusal of the offending director from matters involving you, preservation of all communications and records, and written confirmation within 30 days. Reference Section 209.006's notice-and-cure framework and your Section 209.007 hearing rights to show you are following statutory procedure. Attach evidence—emails, texts, photos, video, witness statements. Make clear that if the conduct continues you will pursue injunctive relief, damages, and any other remedies the law allows against the association and the director. Most Texas HOAs carry directors and officers insurance, and once a written demand arrives, counsel typically gets involved and the harassment stops. The letter also satisfies pre-suit notice requirements and strengthens your position if you later file in justice or district court.
proceduralNotes: Texas justice courts handle small claims up to $20,000, making them a practical venue for damages claims against an HOA or director. Filing fees in justice court typically run $50 to $100. For injunctive relief—an order forcing the harassment to stop—you must file in district court, where filing fees range from $300 to $400. Under Section 209.008, an association may collect attorney's fees from an owner only after written notice that fees will be charged if the delinquency or violation continues, and an owner is not liable for fees incurred before the conclusion of the Section 209.007 hearing, so keep every notice you receive and document your case carefully. The general statute of limitations is four years for breach of fiduciary duty and two years for personal injury or harassment-based tort claims. Section 209.007 lets an owner or the association use alternative dispute resolution services, and in a suit relating to a matter covered by Sections 209.006 and 209.007 a party may move to compel mediation.

faq.q: What counts as harassment by an HOA board member in Texas?
faq.a: Texas does not define HOA harassment in a single statute, but conduct typically includes repeated unwanted contact, threats, selective or retaliatory enforcement, baseless violation notices, surveillance, public shaming at meetings, refusing to honor records requests, and discrimination. Penal Code § 42.07 covers repeated electronic communications sent in a manner reasonably likely to harass, annoy, alarm, abuse, torment, or embarrass another. When a director uses board authority to target you personally rather than enforce rules neutrally, that conduct may also fall short of the director standards in Business Organizations Code Section 22.221.

faq.q: Can I sue an individual board member personally in Texas?
faq.a: Possibly. Texas nonprofit directors must act in good faith, with ordinary care, and in a manner the director reasonably believes to be in the best interest of the corporation (Business Organizations Code Section 22.221). When a director acts outside the scope of board authority, in bad faith, or for personal reasons, a court may find the director did not meet that standard. Claims may include breach of fiduciary duty, intentional infliction of emotional distress, or defamation, depending on the facts. Consult an attorney before naming an individual director.

faq.q: How long does the HOA have to respond to my demand letter?
faq.a: There is no single statutory response deadline for harassment demands, but most demand letters give the HOA about 30 days to respond, and under Section 209.006 an owner may request a board hearing within 30 days after an enforcement notice is mailed. If the association ignores the letter or refuses to act, you can proceed to mediation, file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General's consumer protection division, or sue in justice or district court depending on the relief you seek.

faq.q: Do I have to try mediation before suing my Texas HOA?
faq.a: Not always, but it helps. Section 209.007 of the Texas Property Code provides that an owner or the association may use alternative dispute resolution services, and if a suit is filed relating to a matter covered by Sections 209.006 and 209.007, a party may move to compel mediation. Many HOA governing documents also contain mandatory mediation or arbitration clauses, so check yours. A demand letter is the first step in that process. If the HOA refuses to participate, you preserve the right to file suit.

faq.q: What damages can I recover for HOA board harassment in Texas?
faq.a: Remedies depend on the claim. A court may order injunctive relief to stop the conduct and may award actual damages proven at trial. If discrimination is involved, the Texas Fair Housing Act allows a court to award actual and punitive damages, reasonable attorney fees, court costs, and an injunction (Property Code Section 301.153). Exemplary damages under Chapter 41 of the Civil Practice and Remedies Code require clear and convincing evidence of fraud, malice, or gross negligence (Section 41.003). Association attorney's fees are governed by Section 209.008, which limits when the association may charge them to an owner.
